newsitem.title: FRANCE: France getting back to normal after strike.
newsitem.headline: France getting back to normal after strike.

text.p: France was getting back to normal on Friday after a one-day public sector strike that emboldened one union to push for new protest action next month.
The centre-right government said most workers ignored Thursday's strike call.

But commentators were divided over whether the strike, called by five million civil service workers to protest at government austerity policies for tackling record unemployment, heralded a possible re-run of crippling stoppages of last year.

Some train services were still disrupted on Friday, including in Marseille, Aquitaine and south-east Paris, but SNCF state railways predicted the network would return to normal in most areas by midday.

Other services -- buses, flights, schools, postal services and public administration -- were getting back to normal. The SNCF strike was the longest, lasting until 0600 GMT on Friday from 1800 GMT on Wednesday.
"Traffic is normal on all our lines," said a spokesman for the Paris regional transport authority, which covers the Metro and buses and regional trains.

"A warm-up day," the left-leaning daily Liberation said in a front-page headline, saying the strike was "almost comparable" to one in October 1995 that presaged crippling 24-day stoppages in November and December.

"Strikes: partial mobilisation," the conservative Le Figaro said in a front-page headline on the strikes against staff cuts and austerity aimed at helping France to qualify for a single European currency from 1999.
"'Black Thursday' didn't happen," it said, noting that transport disruption was less than many had predicted. It conceded that unions had rallied tens of thousands for marches.

Civil Service Minister Dominique Perben said just one in three civil servants heeded the strike call, fewer than in a comparable public sector stoppage on October 10, 1995. He offered wage talks to the protesters.

But Louis Viannet, leader of the Communist-led CGT trade union, felt sufficiently encouraged to urge all French unions on Thursday to join him in a new day of nationwide labour protests around November 15.
"We now have the momentum going, which will continue and grow stronger each day," he said on Thursday night.
It was unclear whether he was alluding to a new strike. Unions including the non-partisan Force Ouvriere and the pro-Socialist CFDT have called protests for coming weeks.
Thursday's strike also had wide public support. One newspaper poll showed that 64 percent of voters backed or sympathised with the strikers.

Unlike a public sector stoppage in October 1995, the strike had the overt backing of the opposition Socialist Party. However, France's union movement is divided and lacks a clear rallying theme. Last year union outrage was focused on Prime Minister Alain Juppe's plans to overhaul social security.

Despite big turnout for a march in Paris, it highlighted old divisions in the labour movement over the social security reform. Nicole Notat, head of the pro-Socialist CFDT, faced abuse and attacks in the march.
